On **agent identity**, the guests see a near-term evolution from the current default — "your agent has your permissions" — toward a profile-based system where different personas (work, personal, different projects) carry different access envelopes. The episode's deepest insight is that **adversarial pressure and defensive safety training create a self-improving loop that is now being accelerated by the very agents it seeks to protect**. Shade trains Signal; Signal makes deployments more robust; more robust deployments generate more realistic attack data for continued red teaming. This flywheel is possible only because automated agents can now do the work that previously required expert human labor — and do it at scale.

When Anthropic's Eugene Yan opens his talk with a show of hands asking how many in the audience are security engineers, he is setting up a point that has reshaped the entire vulnerability management landscape: the bottleneck in closing security gaps has moved decisively away from finding bugs and toward everything that happens after discovery. Yan, who has spent months embedding with security teams using Anthropic's Claude Code, presents a framework built on the hard lesson that the hardest problems are no longer technical but organizational.
Yan anchors the episode in two dramatic data points. Mozilla Firefox, which averaged roughly 20 security bug fixes per month in 2025, saw that number triple to 60–70 in February and March 2026, then surge sevenfold to 400 in April 2026 — a 20× jump over the prior-year monthly average. Mozilla attributed about two-thirds of the April fix count (271) to Claude Preview, demonstrating that frontier models can scale vulnerability discovery. Separately, Anthropic (Entropic, as Yan refers to his team) scanned 23,000 open-source repository candidates, found 6,200 rated high or critical, reported 1,600 to maintainers, and saw only about 100 patches pushed upstream. The discovery throughput was no longer the limit; the downstream pipeline was.
## The bottleneck has shifted from discovery to verification, triage, and patching
Yan frames the core insight bluntly: “Finding vulnerabilities now is quite straightforward. The bottleneck has now shifted to verification, triage, and patching.” He argues that any team that invests only in vulnerability scanning—using models to point at potential exploits—will drown in false positives and unprioritized findings. The real leverage comes from building agentic harnesses that can not only find bugs but also confirm they are exploitable, rank them by business impact, and generate validated patches.
The UK AI Security Institute’s cybersecurity benchmark underscores why models can now find more bugs: it measures how long a model can sustain a cybersecurity task (reverse engineering, web exploitation). Yan shows a chart where the 2026 models plotted a step-jump above the prior regression line, indicating a qualitative leap in capability.
## The six-step agentic security loop
Yan distills the workflow that most teams converge on into six steps, which he groups into a setup phase and a loop phase.
### Setup: threat model + sandbox
| Step | Purpose | Key practices |
|---|---|---|
| **Threat model** | Provide model with context it cannot read from code | Bootstrap from docs and past CVE patches; interview system experts; explicitly state compensating controls (e.g., VPN-only, internal service) |
| **Sandbox** | Isolate and reproduce the target environment | VMs with no egress and no production credentials; container-based replicas (app + database + cache + agent) |
A well-documented threat model pushes true-positive rates to 90%+. Yan quotes a CISO: “The model has great context of the code but poor context of the system.” The threat model is the document that captures implicit knowledge—why senior engineers designed something a certain way, which vulnerabilities have been silently mitigated on-call, across which API boundaries the business actually trusts data.
The sandbox must support reproducibility (all agents start from the same container baseline) and safe PoC detonation. One team Yan worked with said their single biggest lever was “having the model test beds essentially sandboxes with live systems where they can run and detonate the PoCs to confirm that they are true positives.”
### Loop: discovery → verification → triage → patching
Yan describes each step in the loop as analogous to a machine-learning pipeline: discovery optimizes for recall, verification for precision, triage for ranking, and patching closes the feedback loop.
**Discovery.** Give the model as much written context as possible, but simplify prompts as models improve—Yan reports he has to cut his prompt size roughly 50% with each new Claude version. The most effective teams also give the model tools (API query tools, log readers, code readers) so it can interact dynamically. One pentesting team that adopted tools achieved “almost 100%” true-positive rates. Yan walks through a minimal example: a five-line Python function that builds a SQL query via string interpolation. Current models spot that instantly.
**Veribration.** Yan stresses that discovery and verification should be separate agents. The discovery agent can self-censor if it also verifies, hurting recall. The verification agent should be independent and adversarial: it receives only the vulnerability report, sees none of the discovery reasoning, and tries to prove the finding is false. It detonates a proof-of-concept in the sandbox. In the SQL injection example, the verification agent runs a curl command and watches customer PII exfiltrate, confirming the exploit.
**Triage.** Triage is where the business context from the threat model becomes critical. Without it, a model might flag a medium-severity issue as high because the database contains healthcare data, but a human reviewer might downgrade it because an application firewall blocks SQL injection and the service is internal-only. Yan shows a two-column table: the agent's initial severity (High, with reasons) and the human-adjusted severity (Low, because of compensating controls). The lesson: product engineers will lose trust if they receive hundreds of medium/low issues. Ranking with the help of the threat model—and written calibration rules agreed upon across security and product teams—is essential.
**Patching.** The patch should meet three criteria: the original exploit stops working, the existing test suite stays green, and a fresh discovery agent reattacks the patched code to ensure comprehensiveness. Yan calls this the “generative verifier loop.” He shows a one-line fix (moving the SQL parameter out of string interpolation) and a second diff that updates the threat model to document the compensating controls, so the next scan iteration is smarter. “When you close the loop, they now become capital expense. You get better with each iteration you run.”

```mermaid
    B --> C["Loop: Discovery"]
    C --> D["Loop: Verification"]
    D --> E["Loop: Triage"]
    E --> F["Loop: Patching"]
    F --> B
```
## Organizational bottlenecks are the hardest ones
Yan warns that technical scaling—spending more compute—is easy. “Human attention doesn’t scale.” He identifies three specific organizational constraints that will break as the agentic pipeline expands:
- **Vulnerability routing.** At dozens of findings per month, manual Jira assignment works. At hundreds, every team needs an automated owner-lookup system (e.g., based on code ownership). This does not require an LLM in the loop.
- **Severity calibration.** Security engineers and product engineers often disagree on what “high severity” means. The only solution is for both sides to sit down, write down the rules once, and feed those rules to the ranking agent.
- **Patching bandwidth.** Yan observes that few professionals at Anthropic still write code by hand, but many still manually construct patches from vulnerability reports. The goal should be AI-generated patches with human validation, using the reattack loop to catch regressions.
“Non-technical problems are an order of magnitude harder than technical problems,” Yan says, citing a former director.
## Getting started now
Yan’s closing advice is concrete and sequential:
1. **Start with open-source dependencies** — a bounded, non-production domain where you can test safely.
2. **Climb the learning curve interactively** — do not aim for automation on day one. Use Claude Code or your favorite IDE, hands-on. “Learn where you get cut. Learn what kind of context you’re missing. Learn where precision is low.”
3. **Do not just scan** — scanning is not the bottleneck. Focus your process design on verification, triage, patching, and the organizational processes around them.
He points to Anthropic’s open-source repositories that include interactive skill definitions and autonomous harness configurations, with a note that step five in the provided set includes a customizable harness.
## Cross-theme synthesis
The episode’s deeper argument is that the AI security pipeline is fast becoming a mirror of every ML pipeline: the returns on model improvements now come not from better raw detection but from better systems engineering around recall, precision, ranking, and closed-loop validation. The threat model document is the equivalent of feature store documentation — the tacit knowledge that lives in engineers’ heads must be externalized or the agent will miss context a human junior engineer would have inferrred automatically. The most brittle constraint Yan identifies is not model capability but organizational alignment on severity. Until security and product teams agree on a shared severity rubric, the agent will produce outputs that neither group trusts. The frontier of AI security work, Yan suggests, may end up being less about code and more about the social engineering of writing down the unwritten rules.

Tariq Shaukat, CEO of Sonar, delivered this talk at an AI engineer conference in July 2026. The central claim is that enterprise-grade AI-assisted development requires verification to be embedded into the development process, not bolted on afterward. Without deliberate verification loops, coding agents generate a surge of technical debt that erodes initial productivity gains within three months. Shaukat introduces the Agent-Centric Development Cycle (AC/DC), a framework of three interlocking loops (agentic, CI verification, code maintenance) built around a “Guide, Verify, Solve” principle, and presents quantitative evidence from Sonar’s own benchmarking and customer deployments.
## The productivity paradox: Initial velocity gains, then decay
Shaukat argues that AI coding agents deliver an undeniable boost in code-production speed, but the quality of the output creates a hidden cost. He cites benchmark data from a third party (Meter) covering “Mythos” models (a leading coding agent at the time). At a 50% success rate, agents can complete a task that would take a human 16–18 hours. But when the accuracy requirement is raised to 80%, the feasible task duration drops to about 3.5 hours. Even at 80%, Shaukat notes, a CTO would put a human delivering that error rate on a performance-improvement plan.
| Success rate | Maximum autonomous task duration (approx.) |
|---|---|
| 50% | 16–18 hours |
| 80% | ~3.5 hours |
The more consequential finding comes from a Carnegie Mellon University study on real-world productivity. Teams using AI coding agents initially saw a 3–5× increase in velocity. Within three months, that advantage vanished. The cause was an increase in security issues, maintainability problems, reliability regressions, and overall code complexity. “You’re building technical debt as quickly as you are generating the code,” Shaukat says, shifting the bottleneck from writing code to verifying and fixing it.
Sonar’s own analysis of code generated by state-of-the-art models (including GPT-55) across 4,000 problems confirms that while functional correctness is high, the generated code still contains bugs and security flaws, and its complexity remains elevated. “The models are amazing at generating very plausible output … but are they correct? And how do you know that they’re correct is a big problem.”
## The “Guide, Verify, Solve” framework
Shaukat argues that the solution is not to stop using agents but to build a disciplined verification system around them. Sonar’s framework has three phases:
- **Guide** – Preemptive verification through context and constraints, so agents produce better code from the start.
- **Verify** – Zero-trust, multi-layered verification applied both during and after code generation.
- **Solve** – Active, verified code maintenance to keep the codebase clean over time.
### Guide: Context and constraints
The “Guide” phase separates context (understanding the existing codebase) from constraints (rules for the new code). Shaukat highlights a new Sonar product called Sonar Vortex, launched the day before this talk (2026-07-19), which provides architectural awareness and semantic navigation maps. Constraints include allowed/forbidden dependencies, coding standards, and intended architecture – not just the current state.
In Sonar’s testing, providing this combination cuts token consumption by over 30% for a given task. “You’re actually making the life of the agent easier,” Shaukat explains.
### Verify: Zero-trust, multi-layered
Verification should assume that every model has biases and different failure modes. Shaukat recommends using multiple models and techniques in a stack:
| Layer | Technique | What it catches |
|---|---|---|
| Algorithmic | Data flow, control flow, pattern matching, secrets detection | Known anti-patterns, security vulnerabilities, misconfigurations |
| Agentic | Intent analysis, business logic checks, “unknown unknowns” | Logical errors, requirements mismatches, hallucinations |
Customers using this multi-layered approach report 44% fewer AI-derived production outages than those who rely on single-layer checks.
### Solve: Verified code maintenance
As agents generate code, technical debt accumulates. Shaukat argues that maintaining clean code is not just a hygiene factor but a compound enabler: agents working on a cleaned codebase consume fewer tokens and less reasoning than agents working on a typical, messy codebase. “If you make the life of the agent easier, if you maintain your codebase, then you’ll actually see compounding effects.” He cites a test with a large bank where applying the full Guide-Verify-Solve approach yielded a 92% reduction in issues compared to using agents without these disciplines.
## The three verification loops
Shaukat diagrams the system as three nested loops, each with a specific verification purpose:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Agentic Loop"] --> B["In-loop verification (context, constraints)"]
    B --> C["Code generation"]
    C --> B
    C --> D["CI Verification Loop"]
    D --> E["PR review (algorithmic + agentic)"]
    E --> F["Quality gates / evals"]
    F --> G["Merge / release"]
    G --> H["Code Maintenance Loop"]
    H --> I["Remediation agents + cleaning"]
    I --> A
```
1. **Agentic loop (inner)** – Verification occurs *as the agent works*, using the context and constraints to prevent problems at the point of generation.
2. **CI verification loop (middle)** – Pull request review that combines algorithmic and agentic checks at high velocity, feeding into quality gates.
3. **Code maintenance loop (outer)** – Continuous, verified remediation and architectural cleanup that keeps the codebase tractable for agents.
“If you neglect verification, you get into a downward spiral pretty quickly. Or you can get into the self-reinforcing loop.” The Carnegie Mellon study illustrates the former; Shaukat’s client data illustrates the latter.
## The enterprise caveat: Why software is not provable
Shaukat is careful to distinguish code (which is provable in isolation) from software (which is complex, messy, full of interdependencies and existing technical debt). “When you start dealing with large code bases, software is not provable.” This is why formal methods alone are insufficient; verification must be a multi-layered system, not a single gate.
He also ties the verification challenge to the broader AI slop problem in professional services, citing high-profile retractions by KPMG and EY and trouble with fabricated legal citations. “The models are incredible at generating things that sound correct. But are they correct? … This is a big problem in professional services … but really, I think if we’re honest, it’s a big problem in every sector.”
## Cross-theme synthesis
Shaukat’s core message is that the adoption of AI coding agents is not a technology problem but a system-design problem. The same speed that creates value also creates waste unless verification is embedded as a first-class function in the development lifecycle. The emerging best practice is not to reject agents or accept slop, but to construct a compounding feedback loop: cleaner code → better agent performance → faster, safer output → cleaner code.
Open questions from the talk: How do these loops scale to billion-line codebases? What is the overhead of running multi-layered verification on every line of agent-generated code – and does it offset the productivity gain? The Sonar framework is a template, but the talk does not compare it against alternatives (e.g., formal verification, prompt engineering alone, human-in-the-loop review). For enterprises already deep into agentic development, the key takeaway is to audit their current code quality trends over the first three months and, if degradation appears, invest in the verification infrastructure before the technical debt becomes unmanageable.

Software engineers who fear that AI coding assistants are automating away the craft have it backward, according to Angie Jones, a prominent AI systems engineer and longtime advocate for testing and quality. Jones spent a Friday night building agents for operational tasks and realized the old "dev flow" thrill was intact — not despite the shift to AI but because of it. The widespread dread that coding assistants are stealing "the fun parts" of software engineering, she argues, is a failure of perspective. Engineering discipline has not been displaced; it has migrated up one layer of abstraction. Designing agentic systems exercises the same muscles — systems thinking, decomposition, workflow design, state management, security engineering — as traditional software, just with different primitives.
Jones grounds the argument in a concrete artifact she built: Relocation Scout, a persistent house-hunting agent. Rather than a one-shot prompt that ranks listings and stops, Relocation Scout is a reusable system with structured memory (implemented via Compendium Wiki), deterministic helper scripts for exact calculations, sub-agents for research tasks, skills that span markets, and human-in-the-loop guardrails for high-stakes actions. Its architecture serves as a live demonstration that building agents is software engineering, and that engineers should let agents handle code-writing grunt work while they reclaim the higher-order design challenge.
## Systems thinking and workflow design
The first engineering skill Jones exercises is **systems thinking**. An agent is not the system, she emphasizes; it is part of a system that includes files, tools, humans, and other agents. Before writing a single prompt, she considers the whole environment: what is this agent's job? What does it depend on? What happens when it breaks? "I want to treat it like any other component where it has boundaries and responsibilities, has dependencies, and ways that it can fail," she says. "That whole thought process, that's engineering."
Relocation Scout does not sit in isolation. It pulls in listings and neighborhood signals, weighs them against the user's criteria, and hands back a ranked shortlist. "What's this agent's job? What does it depend on? What happens if it breaks?" are the questions Jones asks before her coding agent touches a file.
**Workflow design** follows directly. A goal — "review this listing" — is insufficient; an agent needs a path. Jones defines every workflow as containing three phases: **gather** what the agent needs, **weigh** the listing against criteria, and **act**. Every run ends in exactly one of three outcomes: **stop**, **retry**, or **escalate**. That path then shapes the architecture: what context the agent needs, which parts the agent handles directly, and when a tool or human should take over.
```mermaid
graph TD
    A["Goal: Review a listing"] --> B["Workflow phases"]
    B --> C["Gather: collect listing data,<br/>neighborhood signals, criteria"]
    C --> D["Weigh: score against<br/>preferences and rules"]
    D --> E{"Outcome"}
    E -->|Stop| F["Produce shortlist entry"]
    E -->|Retry| G["Reload or re-scrape,<br/>attempt again"]
    E -->|Escalate| H["Hand off to human<br/>for manual review"]
```
## Decomposition and separation of concerns
Giant prompts, Jones argues, are the agentic-system equivalent of a bloated class or single function handling everything. "We scoff when we see one gigantic class or big old function that's doing too much," she says. "We call these code smells. Agentic systems have their own version of this: the giant prompts."
The problem emerges innocently. An instructions file tells Relocation Scout how to size up a listing. An edge case arises, so Jones adds a note. Then a safety rule. Then one more important exception. "Before you know it, that prompt is doing everything. And your engineering spidey sense already knows that this is messy."
Jones decomposes Relocation Scout's original prompt and finds four distinct jobs crammed into one:
| Job hiding in the prompt | Proper home | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Pull and normalize a listing | **Skill** — reusable across agents and markets | Standardized process, single point of change |
| Format the shortlist (fixed output shape) | **Schema / structured output** | Guarantees consistency; matches how any two systems talk |
| Calculate commute time | **Deterministic script** — plain code | Exact answer; LLMs produce drifting, unreliable numbers |
| Research the neighborhood | **Sub-agent** — dedicated, focused scope | Task is meaty enough to warrant its own context; avoids bloating the main agent |
**Decomposition** means spotting distinct jobs and pulling them apart. **Separation of concerns** means putting each responsibility in the right place — the same question Jones would ask in traditional software ("Should this live in the controller or the service layer?"), now asked of agentic primitives: prompt, skill, sub-agent, schema, script.
## Modularity: skills, sub-agents, and the triage of actors
Modularity in agentic systems mirrors modularity in traditional software — reusable functions, classes, libraries — but with different primitives. Jones highlights two.
**Skills** are reusable agent capabilities. Relocation Scout's normalize-listing skill can be dropped into three different city searches without rewriting. "I wrote it once and they all can reuse it," Jones says. "This has now basically become a component that I can reuse across agents or even share with other people — kind of the same way that we lean on packages."
**Sub-agents** are architecturally analogous to functions: given one specific task, called when needed, and scoped narrowly so they do not carry the context of the entire session. The neighborhood-research sub-agent works in any housing market because it does not know about the user's criteria or the shortlist format — only how to research a neighborhood. Not everything should be abstracted, Jones cautions; some instructions are local to a given workflow, and abstraction costs more than it saves when pulled too early. "This is just another engineering decision," she says.
The most structural principle Jones introduces is a **triple triage** for deciding which actor handles which work:
| Actor | Best for | Relocation Scout example |
|---|---|---|
| **Code** | Deterministic, exact-answer tasks | Commute calculation, deduplicating already-seen listings |
| **Agent (LLM)** | Fuzzy judgment, ambiguity, reasoning over messy input | Scoring a listing against preferences, weighing trade-offs |
| **Human** | Authority, binding decisions | Approving a tour booking, submitting an offer |
"Just because an agent *can* do something doesn't mean that it *should*," Jones says. "Some tasks are better handled by plain code. It'll be cheaper, it'll be more reliable. I promise you AI did not invent automation." Her rule of thumb: reach for code when the task has an exact answer; reach for the agent when it needs interpretation or judgment; reach for the human when the decision carries authority.
## Contracts, structured memory, and state management
Free-form text is acceptable when only a human reads the output. When another system must act on an agent's output, a contract — an agreed-upon shape — is required. "We already do this everywhere in software," Jones notes. "Anytime two systems talk, there's an agreed-upon shape between them. Agentic systems need that same discipline."
When Relocation Scout scores a house, it does not just hand back a natural-language message. It writes a structured record — containing a **decision**, a **score**, and a **reason** — into the agent's memory layer, which Jones implements using Compendium Wiki. Because the record is structured, the memory becomes queryable across sessions: "Show me every house rated four or better that has a commute of 15 minutes or less" retrieves specific fields from known locations, not text trapped in a past conversation. The shortlist-generation step also reads these same fields without a human in the loop. "Defining the shape forces you to get really clear and specific," Jones says. "If you can't say what the output should look like, you probably don't yet fully understand what you're asking the agent to produce."
**State management** and **idempotency** follow. Agentic systems operate in messy realities — webhooks fire twice, runs crash mid-step. The agent must track what actions it has already taken. Jones illustrates with Relocation Scout's email-and-calendar flow:
```mermaid
graph TD
    A["New listing scored<br/>above threshold"] --> B["Agent emails realtor<br/>requesting a viewing"]
    B --> C["Agent logs 'email sent'<br/>to memory"]
    C --> D["Agent attempts to<br/>block calendar for tour"]
    D --> E["System crashes"]
    E --> F["Lint pass runs<br/>on recovery"]
    F --> G{"Checks memory:<br/>'email sent' entry exists?"}
    G -->|Yes| H{"Checks calendar:<br/>blocked?"}
    H -->|No| I["Agent blocks calendar<br/>without re-sending email"]
    G -->|No| J["Agent must re-email,<br/>then block calendar"]
```
The trap with LLMs, Jones warns, is that a retry might reword the request just enough to look like a brand-new task. Idempotency must be enforced in the system, not left to the model. "If we run this again, the agent just completes what's missing instead of making a mess."
## Threat modeling and safety boundaries
Security engineering fundamentals apply directly. "We need to validate your inputs, give the least privilege needed, and draw boundaries around what an action can touch," Jones says. "Agentic systems need all of that."
Relocation Scout consumes content from strangers: listing copy from sellers, forum threads, neighborhood reviews from anonymous internet users. All of it is untrusted input. The agent must treat every piece of external text as **evidence, not instructions** — a distinction Jones builds into the prompt explicitly.
Then come **action boundaries**. Relocation Scout can read listings and build shortlists autonomously forever. What it cannot do: email sellers, book tours, or submit offers. Those actions are walled behind human approval. "When you draw that wall, what you've done is reduce the blast radius and minimize your exposure to risk," Jones says. The triad of **validate inputs, least privilege, and blast-radius reduction** maps directly from security engineering to agent design.
## Maintainability as a first-class architectural property
Jones does not have her coding agent design her other agents. "I know it'll be thrown together in a way that technically works, but it's not maintainable," she says. "There's going to be a giant prompt likely, and even if the agent does decompose, I'm not convinced it's going to separate the concerns properly."
She builds maintainability into the system itself. Every level gets an agent-accessible README file that explains the workflow, where the policy lives, and the supporting resources — skills, scripts, sub-agents — and, most critically, **how to keep the agent's memory up to date**. The criterion: any agent, even in a fresh context with no prior session history, can jump into the system and start cold, knowing exactly what to do.
"When I need to modify the system, I can pretty much grab any harness and say, 'Update this agent to do X.' And because the system is so well designed, the chances of it being successful at that update are much higher," Jones says. "If it does happen to run into any issues when trying to update, that's a signal to me that I need to improve the maintainability of the system."
## The constant is building
Jones's closing argument reframes the entire disquiet around AI coding tools. "Designing agents is software engineering. The primitives are different, but the discipline is the same." The list of required skills — understand the system, define the workflow, break the problem down, put responsibilities in the right place, make the right things reusable, determine the best actors for each job, define contracts, manage state, design for safety, make the system understandable — is nearly identical to what every senior engineer already does. "This is why building agents can give you that same thrill of building software. We're still building. We just moved up a layer."
The unresolved tension in Jones's argument, left implicit, is organizational: the engineering discipline she describes — decomposition, idempotency, threat modeling, maintainability — is exactly what many teams currently skip in the rush to ship agentic features. Jones herself admits to adding safety rules and edge-case notes incrementally, exactly the behavior that produces "giant prompts." The systems she builds are engineered by a senior practitioner who deliberately withholds coding-agent autonomy from higher-level architectural decisions. For organizations scaling agent design across dozens of junior engineers, the gap between Jones's practice and the average team's practice may be wide, and the episode offers no prescription for closing it.

Merge co-founders Gil Feig (CTO) and Shensi Ding (CEO) sat down for a 55-minute conversation covering the full sweep of what it means to build AI infrastructure for the enterprise in 2025. Merge, best known as the unified API platform serving OpenAI, Netflix, Uber, Dropbox, Mistral, Perplexity, Freshworks, and JP Morgan among hundreds of other companies, has spent the past 18 months executing a deliberate three-pronged pivot into the AI stack. The episode's central argument — and the finding a busy professional would most miss by skipping it — is that **connecting AI agents to tools is the systemic security nightmare of the next decade**, and that the companies that survive will be those that build hard guard rails around agent-to-data connections, not just smarter models. A secondary but equally urgent claim: the SAS platform model as we know it is structurally threatened by AI coding tools, and enterprise software buyers are already behaving differently.
## The AI Agent Security Nightmare
The core insight Gil Feig returns to repeatedly is that the threat from AI is not the model itself — it is the tools you connect it to. "If you have this sort of evil genius who's a mass murderer but they're locked in a jail cell, they can't do anything. The second you connect it to tools, which is what everyone is trying to do right now, that's where everything goes wrong." This framing reorients the security conversation from model alignment to access governance.
The specific threat vectors Feig and Ding enumerated:
| Threat | Mechanism | Impact |
|---|---|---|
| Supply chain attacks via open source | Agentic code pushed at scale; humans cannot review all PRs | One compromised package infects every downstream codebase |
| Data exfiltration by non-deterministic agents | An agent told "move data from A to B" may also move social security numbers | Sensitive data leaves company boundaries without explicit approval |
| Bot-driven reconnaissance | 1,000+ signups per hour from global IPs scanning all back-end endpoints | Direct breach path; "all it takes is one," says Feig |

Abhishek Bhardwaj, a member of OpenAI's reinforcement learning and agent infrastructure team (and formerly at Google, where he worked on CrosVM, the first Rust-based virtual machine monitor), delivered a 44-minute first-principles architectural briefing on designing a secure, scalable "agent sandbox cloud." The talk, published 2026-07-13, argues that the success of agentic AI — from training loops with verifiable rewards to consumer products like ChatGPT and Codex — is infrastructure-dependent. The central claim is that the industry's "seven stages of grief" in sandbox design converge to a single clear answer: hardware-virtualized micro-VMs for security, block-level incremental snapshotting for durable state, and locality-aware orchestration for latency and cost.
---
## The Motivation: Why Agents Need a Private Linux Box
The foundational problem is that large language models cannot reliably answer verifiable questions (e.g., "how many hours are in strawberry?") because such facts are sparse in training data. The solution is tool calling: the model emits code, a harness executes it, and a grader judges the result. This loop works identically in training (reinforcement learning backpropagation) and in product (inference).
In training, the goal is **throughput** — many parallel rollouts per task to hill-climb toward correct answers. In product, the goal is **latency** — users churn if the sandbox starts slowly. On both sides, the code the model emits is untrusted. It might be intentionally malicious or merely "overzealous" in trying to help (e.g., attempting `getroot` to install a package). Running it directly on the host node risks kernel compromise, exfiltration of model weights or other users' data, and noisy-neighbor resource exhaustion.
Thus a sandbox is required: an isolated environment that gives the model a full Linux computer to drive but blocks attacks on the host kernel and co-tenant workloads.
---
## The Security Spectrum: From `fork` to Hardware Isolation
Abhishek maps the evolution of isolation primitives as a spectrum of escalating security at the cost of performance and complexity.
| Model | Security | Performance | Complexity | Attack Path | Representative Tool |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `fork+exec` | None | Native (fastest) | None | Direct syscalls to host kernel | Raw Unix API |
| Containers | Low–Medium | Near-native | Moderate | Same shared host kernel; seccomp reduces surface but creates whack-a-mole | Docker, LXC |
| gVisor (application kernel) | Medium | Medium (user-space syscall handling) | High | Two-step exploit: compromise Sentry/Gofer, then escalate from there to host kernel | gVisor |
| Micro-VMs (hardware virtualization) | High (hardware boundary) | Lower (VM exit overhead) | Very high | Must chain exploit of KVM plus a device backend (e.g., block, net) | Cloud Hypervisor, Firecracker |
The key insight is that **containers and gVisor share the same host kernel**; a ring-0 exploit inside the container is still a ring-0 exploit on the host. Micro-VMs use the CPU's VMX extensions to create a separate hardware context: the guest kernel runs in ring 0, but inside **VMX non-root** mode. Even a full ring-0 compromise in the guest cannot break into the **VMX root** mode where the host hypervisor (KVM) and the VMM run.

## Micro-VMs: Architecture, Trade-offs, and the Rust Revolution
### How Hardware Virtualization Works
A Virtual Machine Monitor (VMM) — historically QEMU, more recently Rust-based variants — talks to the Linux kernel's hypervisor API (`/dev/kvm`). It allocates guest memory, sets up the kernel and root filesystem, and issues an `ioctl` to launch the guest. Inside the guest, a full Linux boots. When the guest needs to access a hardware resource (a disk block, a network packet), the CPU performs a **VMExit** — a context switch from VMX non-root back to VMX root — and the VMM's device backends (a block thread, a net thread) service the request.
Paravirtualization drivers (Virtio) make this efficient: the guest drivers know they are in a VM and use a shared-memory ring buffer for I/O, reducing the number of exits.
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Host (VMX Root)
        HW["Physical CPU"]
        KVM["/dev/kvm"]
        VMM["VMM Process (e.g., Cloud Hypervisor)"]
        DEV["Device Backends"]
    end
    subgraph Guest (VMX Non-Root)
        APP["User-space App"]
        GKERNEL["Guest Kernel (Ring 0)"]
    end
    VMM -- "ioctl" --> KVM
    KVM -- "VMEntry" --> HW
    HW -- "VMExit" --> KVM
    GKERNEL -- "Virtio I/O" --> DEV
    APP -- "Syscall" --> GKERNEL
```
### The Rust VMM Advantage
For over a decade, QEMU was the standard VMM. It is written in C, supports hundreds of devices and architectures, and has a history of escape vulnerabilities targeting its complex device emulation. Starting in ~2023, a new generation of minimal, Rust-based VMMs emerged:
- **CrosVM** (originally at Google for Chrome OS)
- **Firecracker** (forked from CrosVM; powers AWS Lambda and Fargate)
- **Cloud Hypervisor** (a more general-purpose fork, contributed to by many companies)
Rust eliminates entire classes of memory-safety bugs (buffer overflows, use-after-free) that have historically plagued VMM device emulation. Furthermore, each device backend (block, net) can be jailed with its own seccomp profile and filesystem access, so compromising the block device does not grant access to the network device.
### The Micro in "Micro-VM"
The term refers not to the guest but to the VMM itself. These Rust-based VMMs have a much smaller memory footprint and boot faster because they shed QEMU's historical baggage. A micro-VM can boot a Linux kernel in tens of milliseconds when restored from a memory snapshot.
### Key Trade-offs
- **Performance overhead:** Every VMExit carries a context-switch cost. Disk and network I/O is slower than native or container-based execution.
- **Memory sharing:** The host cannot instantly reclaim guest memory. It must use a balloon driver to ask the guest to relinquish pages, which introduces latency.
- **GPU access:** Direct GPU pass-through (VFIO) is single-tenant per sandbox. Virtio-GPU provides higher-level graphics APIs but not metal access for ML workloads.
- **Security is non-negotiable:** "Security like system tricks can cover performance issues, but they cannot hide security breaches."

## Persistence: The Storage Unlock for Long-Horizon Agents
### Why Disk State Matters
The current default is ephemeral compute: when a sandbox node fails or a model hits a flake, all work (installed packages, generated presentations, GitHub repositories) is lost. This wastes GPU tokens (training) and destroys user trust (product). Abhishek argues that **storage is the next unlock** for agent capabilities, enabling three concrete use cases:
1. **Reliability and scale:** Periodic checkpointing allows transparent migration of a sandbox to a healthy node during cluster upgrades or failures.
2. **Long-running agents:** Models already sustain multi-day tasks (e.g., 3-day Codex "gold mode" sessions). Persistent disk lets them accumulate state indefinitely.
3. **Monte Carlo tree search / backtracking:** A harness can checkpoint a sandbox, explore one branch, restore, and explore another — enabling offline search over solution trajectories.
### Snapshotting Design Choices
| Dimension | Option A | Option B | Abhishek's Recommendation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Granularity | Full snapshot | **Incremental** (diff only) | Incremental — full snapshots at scale are cost-prohibitive and slow |
| Scope | Entire root filesystem | **Configurable workspace** (e.g., `/home`, `/workspace`) | Configurable — base OS rarely changes; only user data needs backup |
| Level | File-level diff (entire files) | **Block-level diff** (changed extents) | Block-level — block maps (`FIE map`) are more efficient than scanning file trees |
| Paradigm | **Explicit** (harness calls `save`) | Always-on (continuous streaming) | Both are useful; explicit is simpler, always-on enables transparent failover |
### Implementation Sketch: Explicit Block-Level Snapshotting
1. **Base image + copy-on-write overlay:** A read-only base image (`base.image`) is shared across all sandboxes. A writable COW overlay is created on top.
2. **Snapshot:** On a `save` API call, `FIE map` (a Linux utility) reports which extents (block ranges) have changed since the last snapshot. Those extents are zipped and uploaded to object storage (S3 / GCS) with a new snapshot ID.
3. **Async optimization:** The snapshot API returns the ID immediately; the upload happens in the background. The harness is not blocked.
4. **Restore:** Given a snapshot ID, the system resolves its lineage (base + layers), downloads only the layers not already cached on the chosen node, applies them on top of the base image, and boots the micro-VM.
### Implementation Sketch: Always-On Persistence
The sandbox sees a local block device (via NBD — Network Block Device). This device is backed by a user-space filesystem that implements a tiered cache:
- **L1:** In-node DRAM (hot blocks)
- **L2:** In-cluster distributed cache (e.g., Redis or local SSDs on nearby nodes)
- **L3:** Object storage (cold, durable)
All writes are acknowledged once committed to the in-cluster tier (L2), ensuring durability across single-node failures without the harness having to call `save`.
---
## Orchestration: Low-Latency Fleet Management
Running sandboxes across the globe requires a control plane that selects a cluster (based on region, load, proximity to the model serving harness) and a scheduler that selects a node within that cluster. The core design challenge is **latency**: a sandbox must be ready in milliseconds, not seconds.
### Acceleration Techniques
| Technique | Latency | Cost (idle resources) | Complexity |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Pre-warmed pool** | Lowest (instant) | High (VMs consume CPU/RAM while idle) | Low |
| **JIT memory snapshot restore** | Low (~tens of ms) | None (no idle VMs) | High (requires memory snapshot infrastructure) |
| **Hybrid** | Low (warm pool refreshes from snapshot) | Medium | Medium |
In the hybrid approach, a small warm pool absorbs immediate requests. When the pool is exhausted, new sandboxes are created from a memory snapshot (booted in ~30ms instead of the ~2s needed for a full kernel boot).
### Locality-Aware Scheduling via Snapshot Layers
Because incremental snapshots produce a lineage of layers, restoring a sandbox is fastest on a node that already caches most of those layers. The scheduler scores candidate nodes by counting how many of the required snapshot layers are already present on their local disks.

## Cross-Theme Synthesis and Open Questions
The briefing maps a coherent architectural stack for agent infrastructure. The foundational layer is hardware virtualization for security, not because it is the most performant, but because security failures are unrecoverable brand and trust events. The second layer is block-level, incremental persistence that treats sandbox state as a durable asset rather than an ephemeral byproduct. The third layer is a latency- and locality-aware control plane that treats state locality as a first-class scheduling signal.
Three open areas remain:
1. **GPU pass-through for training sandboxes:** Direct metal access (VFIO) is single-tenant. Multi-tenant GPU sharing inside micro-VMs is an unsolved problem. Virtio-GPU provides only high-level API access, insufficient for the low-level CUDA operations used in RL training rollouts. Abhishek acknowledges this as a limitation without offering a clear path forward.
2. **The performance tax of VM exits on I/O-bound agents:** Agents that compile code, run databases, or perform heavy filesystem operations will pay the VMExit penalty on every device access. Whether the overhead is acceptable depends on the agent's workload profile and the effectiveness of the paravirtualized Virtio drivers.
3. **Warm-pool sizing for low-latency products at ChatGPT/Codex scale:** The hybrid approach (warm pool + JIT snapshot restore) requires predictive scaling logic that is not detailed in the talk. Over-provisioning wastes GPU-equivalent dollars; under-provisioning causes cold starts that users will perceive.
The episode s central finding is a direct challenge to engineers currently building agent infrastructure on containers or custom runtime isolation: the seven stages of sandbox grief end with micro-VMs. Start there.

Erik Meijer, a research scholar at Leibniz Labs, delivered a sharp 21-minute diagnosis of the AI agent safety crisis at a 2026 AI engineering conference, followed by a concrete, type-theoretic cure. His core claim: the industry is about to let the general public hand control of their computers, finances, and personal lives to AI agents without any protection, because the standard approach—letting models call tools directly—is catastrophically unsafe. The solution is not better alignment or more guardrails; it is a return to first principles from 1990s programming languages research: proof-carrying code. Meijer’s argument is structured as a progression from tool-call danger → deferred execution → reified plans → provable safety, using only elementary type systems and compiler knowledge.
Meijer sets the stage with a personal anecdote: while “vibe coding” for the talk, he accidentally allowed Claude Code to delete one of his files. To him, this is not an accident—it is a feature of models that “do everything that they can to reach that goal, including killing us or deleting your files.” He frames the entire arc of LLM deployment as a series of escalating risks, each met with insufficient responses.
---
## From Magic to Pandora’s Box: The Tool-Call Inflection Point
The launch of ChatGPT on November 30, 2022, felt magical—a user could finally talk to a computer in natural language. But that thin interface (`LLM(question) → answer`) opened Pandora’s box. Prompt injection—where the model cannot distinguish code from text—reintroduced a problem the industry thought it had cured after the “smallpox of SQL injection.” Meijer calls it “bigger than SQL injection ever was.”
The real catastrophe arrived in June 2023, when OpenAI added tool-call support to GPT-4. Every other vendor copied it instantly, Meijer notes, invoking “the principle of minimum differentiation.” Adding tool calls changed AI safety from a philosophical debate about offensive words into a concrete, irreversible risk: the model can now execute side effects while generating an answer.
| Phase | Interface | Problem | Risk level |
|-------|-----------|---------|------------|
| Raw LLM (pre‑2023) | `LLM(question) → answer` | Prompt injection, offensive output | Philosophical – words alone |
| Aligned LLM (mid‑2023) | Requires `proper(question)`, ensures `safe(answer)` | Safety is not a mathematical property; models still jailbroken | Medium – still just words |
| LLM + Tool Calls (June 2023 onward) | `LLM(question) → IO[answer]` | Side effects (delete files, drain bank accounts) during computation | High – real-world damage |
Meijer’s signature joke: AI safety was “just a philosophical debate” when models only produced words, because “some human has to act on words to make them dangerous.” Tool calls “give the model claws in addition to a mouth”—or “a loaded gun.” The type signature changed from returning an answer to returning an `IO[answer]`, where `IO` in Lean (the formal verification system he uses for illustration) is annotated with a `RealWorld` type. This warns the programmer that the computation can mutate the world irreversibly. “If you get a safe answer but all your files are gone, who cares about the safe answer?”
---
## The “Lethal Trifecta” and the Failure of Alignment
Meijer credits Solomon Hikes—who defined an AI agent as “an LLM that’s wrecking its environment in a loop”—and Simon Wilson’s “lethal trifecta”: agents have access to **private data**, they receive **untrusted content** (prompt injections), and they wield **tools**. All three together guarantee exploitation.
The industry’s response has been inadequate:
- **Alignment baked into model weights** – can be jailbroken routinely.
- **LLMs as judges** – 100+ startups in the exhibition hall use an external LLM to judge safety of outputs. But safety is not a formal property; it cannot be proven.
- **Lean-based formal verification** – PhD researchers slapped a Lean proof on the LLM interface: `requires proper(question) ensures safe(answer)`. Meijer calls this “impossible to write a formal proof for” because “safe” is not a mathematical property. “That is why there are at least 100 startups down here in the exhibition hall that are using LLMs as a judge.”
He shows a Lean signature that tries to guarantee safety, then immediately dismisses it: “If you think about this for a single nanosecond, you will realize that it’s impossible to write a formal proof that an answer is safe or a question is proper.” The only real solution, he says, is to stop trying to embed safety into the model and instead **air-gap the agent from its ability to act**.
---
## Deferring Execution: The “Left, Left, To the Right, Right” Maneuver
Meijer’s core technical insight is to push the `IO` side effect to the right side of the interface. Instead of the agent executing the agentic loop itself, it **returns a plan** for execution. The plan is of type `IO[answer]`, but because it is a *value* (not an effect), it can be inspected and proven safe before execution.
He illustrates with a dance: “We are pushing this IO to the right, to the right. And what you now see is that the tool belt of Claude goes to the left, to the left, and suddenly Claude is a nice puppy again.” The model now creates a plan; a trusted runtime (personified as “Bernie”) executes it.
The Lean manual says `IO` is a black box – you cannot reason about it. So the next step is to **reify the plan into a program**, an expression that represents the computation. Meijer introduces the **free monad**: a monad “that loves type classes.” By representing the agent’s actions as an algebraic data type, the model returns an expression of type `Expr[IO[answer]]`. Compiler courses teach that programs are trivial to analyze: data-flow analysis, taint checking, type checking – all become straightforward.
A simple inductive interpreter and an inductive proof over the expression language can now be generated by the model itself. “You now have a simple inductive recursive interpreter for this language and you have a simple inductive proof – and the models can generate these proofs.”
---
## Proof-Carrying Code: Stealing from the 1990s
“I’m my brain is the size of a peanut,” Meijer jokes. “This is something called proof-carrying code, invented by academics in the 1990s, and I’m just stealing it.”
| Traditional agent | Safe agent (proof-carrying) |
|------------------|-----------------------------|
| Model calls tools directly | Model returns a program (expression) |
| Side effects happen during generation | Side effects are deferred |
| Cannot inspect effects before they happen | Program can be statically analyzed |
| Safety is assumed via alignment | Safety is mathematically proven |
| Black-box IO | White-box free monad |
The flow becomes:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["User Request"] --> B["LLM (Claude)"]
    B --> C["Plan (Free Monad Expr)"]
    C --> D["Proof-Carrying Code Verifier"]
    D --> E{"Safe?"}
    E -->|Yes| F["Trusted Runtime Executes"]
    E -->|No| G["Block Execution"]
    F --> H["Answer"]
    G --> I["Alert / Sanitize"]
```
Meijer explicitly updates the three-point summary for the audience:
1. **Agents are dangerous until proven safe.** Never let agents act unless you can absolutely prove safety.
2. **The language is for machines, not humans.** Normal users don’t need to understand free monads. The same machine generates the plan, proves it, and consumes it. “We should stop designing languages for humans” for this use case.
3. **All basic stuff – requires Programming 101 only.** Proof-carrying code, type systems, free monads are foundational CS.
He notes that a group of academics, now including himself at Harvard, have implemented a working version on GitHub, using a slightly different language but the same principle. “The language doesn’t matter – it’s the principle that matters.”
---
## Cross-theme Synthesis and Open Questions
Meijer’s talk is deliberately provocative, but it rests on a genuine engineering insight: the mainstream agentic architecture is unsafe by construction, and the fix is not more data or compute but a decades-old idea from formal verification. The biggest unresolved tension is whether this approach can scale to real-world, open-ended agentic tasks where the set of tools and interactions is unbounded. Proof-carrying code works when the action space is known statically; dynamic tool invocation (e.g., calling arbitrary APIs discovered at runtime) breaks the assumption. Meijer does not address this in the talk.
A second open question: who is “Bernie”? The trusted runtime requires that the execution environment itself is tamper-proof. If the runtime is compromised, the proofs are moot. Meijer leaves the runtime’s security unaddressed.
Finally, the talk implies that foundation-model labs are uninterested in this approach because it slows down deployment and commoditizes their models. If safety can be provided entirely by a formal verification layer wrapped around any LLM, then the model itself becomes a commodity plan-generator. This threatens the moat of companies like OpenAI and Anthropic, which sell safety as a product feature. Meijer’s answer: “Hopefully next year you will have a booth downstairs where you have created a provably safe agentic harness.” The opportunity is for startups, not incumbents.
**What to watch in 2026–2027:**
- Whether the Harvard codebase or a commercial derivate (e.g., a “Claude Safety Harness”) gains traction.
- Whether Anthropic or OpenAI adopt deferred execution and proof-carrying code in their agent APIs, or continue to defend the direct-tool-call model.
- Regulatory attention: if a well-publicized agent disaster occurs in consumer finance or healthcare, Meijer’s thesis will become the default regulatory template.

The gap between frontier large language models is narrowing faster than the hype suggests — especially when evaluated within agentic harnesses rather than on static benchmarks. In this episode, co-hosts Michael Watson and Jhanvi Virani (co-founders of Hedgineer) dissect the strategic implications of this convergence, drawing on hands-on enterprise work and a research sponsorship with Lehigh University's Master of Financial Engineering program. They argue that while raw model performance is becoming commoditized, the real differentiators now lie in ecosystem architecture: token speed, memory management, open standards like MCP, and the willingness to prioritize value over premature vendor-agnosticism. The episode offers a practical framework for navigating the frontier model race without strategic paralysis.
## The Convergence of Frontier Models in Agentic Tasks
Michael describes a series of evaluations run with the Harbor framework, comparing models under the same agentic harness (Claude Code). The key finding: "If you use the same agentic harness and just swap out the underlying model across different problems… there's not that significant of a difference." This challenges the common belief that model quality differences observed in LLM leaderboards carry over to agentic workflows. The team used a proxy stack (Claude Code proxy on top of LLM light) to route Anthropic's agent harness through other providers like OpenAI and Gemini, with essentially no cost to the harness itself — inference spend alone accounts for the cost.
| Provider | Representative Model | Relative Speed | Relative Cost | Quality Gap in Agentic Harness |
|----------|---------------------|----------------|---------------|--------------------------------|
| Anthropic | Claude Sonnet/Opus | Baseline | Baseline | Baseline (excellent tool use) |
| OpenAI | GPT-4o | Higher | Lower | Small or negligible |
| Google | Gemini 3.5 Flash | Very high | Lower | Small or negligible |
| DeepSeek | (not specified) | Comparable | Lower | Small |
| Cerebras (inference chip) | Any model | ~10x faster than Anthropic | Not disclosed | Same model quality |
> "The new model to me is turning into the least interesting update… what gets me excited is tokens per second." — Jhanvi Virani
The implication: model selection decisions should weight inference speed and total cost far more heavily than capability deltas, especially once an agent harness and tool infrastructure are in place. Cerebras's recent IPO on this thesis — a chip architecture designed purely for inference — validates the market's bet on speed as a differentiator.
## Anthropic's Strategy: Doubling Down on Enterprise Agentic Infrastructure
Anthropic's developer-day announcements reveal a company laser-focused on enterprise token consumption, while deliberately ceding revenue from adjacent compute and storage. Two flagship features:
- **Self-hosted managed agents**: The agent harness runs inside Anthropic's environment, but all tool execution occurs in the client's own containerized environment via MCP. This means Anthropic never touches client data or compute — they only bill for tokens consumed in reasoning and tool-selection.
- **Open memory stores and skills**: Memories are stored as plain text files in GitHub. Skills are version-controlled in GitHub repos. "Dreaming" (periodic condensation of session memories) is also run as a standard agentic process, removing duplicates and synthesizing context. Everything is portable.
> "They're really doubling down and they want to compete on token quality… they don't care about anything that's built on top of their agentic loop." — Michael Watson
This architecture stands in deliberate contrast to hyperscalers like Google or AWS, which embed model inference inside broader compute ecosystems (BigQuery, GCP) to capture spend at multiple layers. Anthropic's bet is that enterprises will pay a premium for inference quality as long as they retain ownership of data and tool logic.
## Memory Stores and Recursive Learning: The Next Frontier in Context Management
Jhanvi explains memory stores with a concrete instruction: "Any time you make a mistake and I correct you, write it down." The agent appends a new text file to a folder in GitHub each time the instruction triggers. "Dreaming" is then applied periodically: a separate agent reads the entire store, condenses it into a cleaned, deduplicated, synthesized version, and overwrites the store.
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["User session with agent"] --> B["Instruction: write mistake to memory"]
    B --> C["Memory Store (text files in GitHub)"]
    C --> D["Dream agent (periodic)"]
    D --> E["Condensed Memory Store"]
    E --> F["Next session loads condensed context"]
```
Because the store is pure text in a git repo, it is model-agnostic by construction. Michael notes that this is the same concept as the "recursive learning model" discussed with a previous guest (Mitch), where agents decide what to retain in context. Anthropic's implementation is clean but not proprietary — the same format could be read by OpenAI or any other provider. This portability is a critical let-down for lock-in fears.
## Google IO: A Scattershot Push into Consumer AI
Jhanvi summarizes three announcements from Google's developer day that signal a different priority:
- **Gemini 3.5 Flash**: Faster but reviews mixed on quality parity with Sonnet/Opus.
- **Spark**: An AI assistant embedded across Google Workspace (Gmail, Docs, Slides) — a consumer-facing agent that spans the full product suite.
- **Omni model**: A multimodal input/output system — takes video, audio, code and outputs any format. Current version constrained to audio/video output but designed to expand.
> "They seem a little scatterbrained… but I think this is just the beginning of what consumer AI will be." — Jhanvi Virani
The strategic contrast with Anthropic is sharp: Google leverages its massive consumer product surface area, while Anthropic builds deep infrastructure for professional workflows. The episode does not predict a winner but observes that the two strategies are complementary rather than directly competitive — at least for now.
## Vendor Lock-In: A Bell Curve of Concern
The question of lock-in — "Is it dangerous to commit to one frontier model?" — is the episode's most practical through line. Michael and Jhanvi classify firms into three stages:
| Stage of AI Adoption | Typical Lock-In Fear | Correct Action |
|----------------------|----------------------|----------------|
| Left of bell curve (experimentation) | High, but premature | Pick one ecosystem, get ROI first |
| Middle of bell curve (building stack) | Moderate | Use open standards (MCP, skills, telemetry) to preserve optionality |
| Right of bell curve (full integration) | Justified and valid | Build observability layer; own all session data via open telemetry |
> "If you're not even getting any ROI out of it in the first place, why worrying about vendor locking doesn't matter." — Michael Watson
The hosts draw an extended analogy with the early cloud era: firms that delayed cloud adoption out of lock-in fear lost years of productivity. Similarly, trying to be "cross-model" from day one adds unnecessary complexity. The realistic path is to commit, get value, then use open standards — which the ecosystem now provides (MCP, skill libraries in GitHub, OpenTelemetry) — to enable later switching at lower cost.
Jhanvi adds that for end users (non-technical staff), having all context in one ecosystem (e.g., conversations, memories) is far more valuable than split usage across ChatGPT and Claude. The cost of switching is also designed to decline over time as competitors build import tools.
## Cross-Theme Synthesis and Open Questions
The convergence of model quality in agentic tasks, combined with the openness of Anthropic's infrastructure, suggests that enterprises should focus on building durable skill libraries, memory stores, and observability — not on model purity. The real vendor lock-in risk is not the model itself but the proprietary data formats around session history and context. By keeping those in standard formats (GitHub, OpenTelemetry), firms can treat model selection as a tunable cost variable.
An open tension remains: as Google and OpenAI embed deeper into their own compute ecosystems (BigQuery, Azure), their ability to subsidize tokens against other revenue could undercut Anthropic's pure-token pricing. Anthropic's bet depends on enterprises valuing open data ownership enough to accept a potential price premium. The next 12 months — and the competitive response from Google's Omni model — will test that thesis.

In a wide-ranging conversation recorded at the AI Engineer (AIE) conference in early July 2026, swyx — the conference's founder and longtime developer evangelist (previously at Netlify, AWS, and a prolific voice in the front-end ecosystem) — and Matthew Berman, a prominent AI YouTuber and commentator, dissected the state of frontier model development, the geometry of application-layer startups, and the long odds of aligned artificial general intelligence. The episode functioned less as an interview and more as a rapid-fire peer-level debate about what engineers should actually bet on when the technology moves three times a year. The central tension running through the conversation: the rapid iteration of frontier models simultaneously empowers engineers and threatens to obliterate their products — and the only sustainable response is to own a specific human problem, not a specific model.
## From front-end to AI: the professionalization thesis
Swyx located the origin of the AIE conference in a pattern he had observed across three earlier disciplines. Front-end engineering, cloud engineering, and data engineering each matured into professionalized fields with dedicated conferences, influencers, and toolchains. He bought the domain `ai.engineer` in late 2023, wrote a manifesto blog post, and planned the first conference. The early boost came from Andre Karpathy's endorsement — a signal that the thesis had credibility.
> "I had seen basically front-end engineering become its own professionalized field with dedicated conferences, dedicated influencers and tech stacks... I was like it's very obviously going to happen to AI."
The first edition (2024) was the hardest: no history, no word-of-mouth. Swyx partnered with Ben (founder of Reactathon, a West Coast React conference) who handled logistics while swyx curated content. The value proposition that now attracts every frontier lab — OpenAI, Anthropic, etc. — is neutral ground. Labs compete on the same stage, which swyx argues is **maximally beneficial for engineers and most competitive for the labs**. A lab's own dev day cannot replicate that dynamic.
## Inference silicon moves beyond Nvidia
Swyx attended an hour-long session on **etched**, which came out of stealth that week (from the perspective of the recording, week of July 6, 2026). He framed etched as "next-generation Cerebras" — a chip dedicated specifically to the post-transformer workload that dominates today's LLM inference. Cerebras started 10+ years ago and recently held its IPO; like Groq, it was designed before the transformer era. Etched and others (Madix) are optimized for the architecture that has been largely stable since GPT‑3.5 / ChatGPT.
> "All of inference is just so goddamn big that of course you're going to have A6 for inference."
The risk of custom chips being obsoleted by architectural shifts (e.g., a new model type) is real, but swyx is sanguine: existing workloads don't vanish. Companies that build on current models tend to keep them running once they work. Nvidia will continue to build GPUs, but the inference market is large enough to sustain multiple silicon players.
## Frontier-lab behavior: pricing, capacity, and government ties
### Anthropic and the Fable model
The conference featured an Easter-egg game built with Anthropic's **Fable** model (a reference to the fictional "Fable" as a code name). Berman noted the widespread narrative that Anthropic was compute-constrained and had throttled rollout of Opus and Fable. Swyx pushed back:
> "They know their roadmap. It probably wasn't true a month ago... they probably already knew these compute deals were coming."
He pointed to the recently announced partnerships with AWS and xAI as long-planned — the delays were more likely safety-related than capacity-related. On Fable's quality, swyx observed: "When it works, it is extremely smart, but it's also very slow." He has used it in Cursor and found it slightly faster than the initial release, but the slowness means he only uses it for the hardest problems. False refusals still occur, though swyx said he has not encountered rerouting to Opus.
Both speakers agreed that **capability overhang** from the previous generation (Opus, GPT‑5.5) remains large — most customers do not fully exploit those models. The current generation (GPT‑5.6, Fable) adds even more headroom. Engineers live in the "white space" between peak capability and broad deployment.
### OpenAI's rumored 5% equity offer to the US government
A few days before the recording, a story broke (unconfirmed) that OpenAI had proposed giving the U.S. government a 5% equity stake. Swyx called the idea plausible. He contrasted it with the American tradition of arms-length government: "I'm from Singapore. Temasek and GIC own significant portions of the Singapore economy, and it works just fine." His interpretation:
- The move gives the public a share in the upside, preventing a permanent underclass.
- It aligns national interest with the lab's success.
- It may be a tactical "art of the deal" gambit: start extreme and negotiate back.
- The government's motivations (national security, economic share, safety) all converge, making it hard to isolate any single driver.
| **Possible motivation** | **Swyx's comment** |
|------------------------|-------------------|
| National security / preventing hostile AI in adversarial hands | "Most afraid of" – these all align |
| Economic share for citizens | "People of the United States do need to have a share or a say in some upside" |
| Safety regulation via ownership stake | Governance without legislation |
## Regulation and the utility question
Swyx argued it is too early to regulate AI as a utility. He drew an analogy to Thomas Edison's early electricity experiments — no one would have regulated electric light as a utility in 1882.
> "It's a little unfair... four years after ChatGPT to be like, no, we should regulate it now like a utility because there's no more innovation to be had."
The White House is currently exerting hands-on control over model release timing (e.g., GPT‑5.6 required a weeks-long delay after announcement). Swyx sees this as a necessary national framework to avoid a patchwork of state laws, citing California's SB‑47 as a previous attempted regulation that was worse. He also called out the "multi-turn game" of politics: this administration's approach will not bind its successor.
## P(doom): existential risk over different horizons
Swyx revealed his personal probabilities of human extinction or severe disempowerment from AI, but insisted that p(doom) must be **attached to a timeline** or it is meaningless.
| Horizon | swyx's P(doom) estimate | Context |
|---------|--------------------------|---------|
| 10 years | ~5%* | "Near zero" initially; later revised down from 10% to 5% |
| 50 years | Implicitly >5% (end of lifetime) | Not given a number |
| 50,000 years (approx lifespan of *Homo sapiens*) | ~90% | "We don't have a right to exist anymore than anything else" |
*The exact figure is ambiguous. He says "Poom in 10 years is near zero", then later "throw out 10 [percent]. No, 10's too high. Five%." The final calibrated estimate appears to be 5% on a 10-year horizon.
He resonated with the evolutionary perspective from *Foundation* and *Dune*: "Who are we to say that we happen to live in the exact moment that everything ends?" He also distinguished AIE from EAC (Effective Altruism conferences) — EAC focuses exclusively on AGI timelines and existential risk, while AIE is pragmatic, optimistic but not unconstrained, and incorporates guardrails, evals, and systems engineering.
## Agent labs and the application-layer playbook
The most actionable insight in the episode was swyx's concept of **"agentlab"** — a startup that positions itself as "the AI guy" for a specific customer vertical. He laid it out in a blog post (`latent.space/agentlabs`). The core philosophy:
- Don't pick a solution; pick a problem.
- Become the trusted brand that always applies the latest AI to that problem, absorbing model changes on behalf of the customer.
- Accept that product categories will be eliminated periodically; build the capacity to pivot to the new capability overhang.
Examples cited: Cursor, Cognition, Decagon, Harvey. All are agentlabs for coding, large‑enterprise software, customer support, and legal respectively.
A significant debate emerged about **model routing** (using multiple models for cost or capability) vs **deep integration with one model**. Swyx argued:
> "If you pride yourself on routing, you will never exploit the full capabilities of one because you're not all in on one... [you become] lowest common denominator of every model out there."
He observed that top-tier agent builders maximize every feature the model provides: prompt caching, tool use, full API surface, discounts from volume. Routing is a marketing line, not a technical edge. However, he acknowledged that the frontier labs themselves may eventually dominate application layers if they generalize sufficiently — the hedge is to stay nimble.
## The conference ecosystem as a strategic asset
AIE has now established itself as the neutral ground where frontier labs compete for developer mindshare. Swyx reflected on the difficulty of the first conference — building enough trust for people to show up — and the advantage of the second: word of mouth, the YouTube channel, and a clear track record. The conference's content spans the full stack, from end‑user applications down to chips (etched) and world‑model research.
## Cross-theme synthesis
The episode surfaced a deep strategic tension for anyone building on AI: the technology advances so quickly that full exploitation of one model is both a competitive advantage and a vulnerability. Agentlabs that go deep with one model (e.g., Cognition on Anthropic) outperform those that abstract across many, but they also bet on the continued leadership of that provider. Meanwhile, the government is moving closer to the frontier labs, via equity stakes and direct release oversight, which could reshape the competitive landscape in ways engineers cannot control. The pragmatic takeaway: pick a vertical, own the problem, and stay ready to re‑implement as models evolve. The chip layer, too, is fragmenting — etched and its peers suggest that the future of inference may be more diverse, not less. And the existential horizon remains long enough that near‑term product thinking is rational, even for someone who thinks humanity has a ~90% chance of eventual disempowerment on a evolutionary timescale.

ai_security.title: Dense-Sparse Dynamic Time Warping for Customizing Piano Concerto Accompaniments
ai_security.abstract: In this study, we explore how pianists can customize Music Minus One (MMO) concerto accompaniments to match their playing style. Bypassing the need for a symbolic score, often not available digitally, we use three types of audio data: solo piano recordings, MMO orchestra-only recordings, and mixed recordings of both piano and orchestra (e.g., from YouTube). The mixed recording serves as an intermediary reference to align the solo and orchestra parts, with only the orchestral part being adjusted through time-scale modification to synchronize with the user's playing. The main challenge with estimating these alignments is the spectral mismatch between recordings containing different musical parts. Motivated by this application scenario, we introduce Dense-Sparse DTW, a variant of Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) that is designed to improve robustness of alignments to spectral mismatch by focusing on aligning a selected subset of audio frames containing prominent timing cues. We collect and annotate data from four piano concerto movements and establish a framework for generating and evaluating customized accompaniment recordings. On this benchmark, we show that Dense-Sparse DTW has better or comparable performance than more complex approaches based on source separation and spectral subtraction techniques.

ai_security.title: HOMIE: Human-object Centric Video Personalization via Multimodal Intelligent Enchancement
ai_security.abstract: Human-object centric video personalization (HOCVP) is a core task within subject-driven video generation. However, existing methods suffer from two key limitations. First, most approaches focusing on inter-subject personalization still struggle to strike a balance between high subject fidelity and accurate interaction patterns between humans and diverse objects, especially when objects represent abstract concepts such as logos. Second, while intra-subject references (e.g., OCR maps, multi-view inputs) are expected to enhance subject fidelity, most existing works lack mechanisms to understand such latent correspondence. To address both challenges, we propose HOMIE, an HOCVP framework that tackles both inter- and intra-subject input settings in a unified manner. Compared to previous approaches, HOMIE proposes a better MLLM integration strategy to extract knowledge of reference-level relationships without compromising the controllability of text encoders or incurring costly re-alignment. Specifically, we introduce global multimodal guidance within self-attention to better align MLLM-derived semantic features with VAE tokens. Furthermore, we propose modality-reference embedding to differentiate tokens from MLLM features and VAE tokens and associate intra-subject reference image tokens. Extensive experiments validate that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance across various HOCVP tasks. Project Page: https://yiyangcai.github.io/homie-page.github.io/

ai_security.title: Distilled Reinforcement Learning for LLM Post-training
ai_security.abstract: Large language model (LLM) post-training is essential for improving reasoning, adaptation, and alignment. Existing methods mainly follow two paradigms: reinforcement learning (RL) and on-policy distillation (OPD). However, RL relies on coarse-grained outcome supervision, resulting in difficult credit assignment and limited capability to acquire new knowledge. OPD, meanwhile, unconditionally matches teacher logits through KL divergence, which creates a dilemma: similar teachers provide little new knowledge, while substantially different teachers often yield ineffective guidance, largely restricting OPD to within-family distillation. We propose Distilled Reinforcement Learning (Distilled RL), which integrates teacher supervision into the RL objective to provide fine-grained guidance, selectively transfer new knowledge and avoid unconditional imitation. Distilled RL contains three components: reverse importance sampling with clipping, negative sample reset, and sequence-level geometric normalization. Through a concise and interpretable case study, we demonstrate that Distilled RL can effectively transfer previously unavailable knowledge from a teacher model to a student model. Extensive experiments across both within-family and cross-family distillation settings show that Distilled RL substantially outperforms standard RL and OPD in terms of both pass@1 and pass@k. Our code is available at https://github.com/597358816/Distilled-RL.

ai_security.title: Can Multimodal Large Language Models Understand OCT?
ai_security.abstract: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) imaging is essential for the diagnosis and treatment of retinal diseases. Although multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated considerable potential in medical image analysis, existing benchmarks largely reduce OCT understanding to coarse-grained disease classification or isolated visual question answering, leaving the complete cognitive process from visual perception to clinical reasoning insufficiently evaluated. To address this limitation, we introduce OCT-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark dedicated to OCT image understanding. OCT-Bench comprises 10,076 high-quality multiple-choice questions constructed from 4,137 OCT images across seven public datasets. Following the real-world clinical interpretation workflow, we establish a hierarchical capability taxonomy consisting of 20 fine-grained tasks across three dimensions: Perception, Cognition, and Reasoning. These tasks cover a broad range of capabilities, including imaging attributes, retinal anatomy, lesion characteristics, spatial relationships, disease assessment, therapeutic decision-making, and prognostic management. We systematically evaluate 20 representative MLLMs, including proprietary models, open-source general-purpose models, and medical-domain models. Experimental results demonstrate that current models remain substantially short of reliable OCT understanding. Moreover, neither medical-domain adaptation nor increased model scale consistently improves performance across capability levels. OCT-Bench enables comprehensive and fine-grained evaluation of MLLMs, providing a foundation for identifying capability bottlenecks and advancing clinically grounded OCT understanding.

ai_security.title: Group Entropy-Controlled Policy Optimization
ai_security.abstract: Entropy control has become an effective tool in reinforcement learning (RL) of large language models (LLMs), helping balance exploration-exploitation trade-off during alignment process. Such RL paradigm is often conducted on mixtures of heterogeneous tasks, which induce distinct entropy regimes under the same policy, making global or token-level entropy regulation insufficient to corresponding heterogeneous needs of exploration. This heterogeneity further makes GRPO-style normalized advantages induce an entropy-dependent bias, making advantage signals across prompt groups statistically non-comparable. To address this issue, we propose Group Entropy-Controlled Policy Optimization (GEPO), a lightweight extension to GRPO that uses group entropy, estimated from existing grouped samples to perform entropy-conditioned asymmetric advantage shaping. GEPO attenuates positive advantages in low-entropy groups to reduce over-exploitation, and negative advantages in high-entropy groups to preserve exploration, with adaptive thresholds derived from historical entropy statistics. Extensive experiments on two base models across thirteen benchmarks spanning mathematics, physics, science, code generation, and instruction following show that GEPO consistently outperforms GRPO and recent entropy-controlled methods, delivering balanced cross-task improvements while preserving task-specific exploration levels throughout training.
